heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ།
source: སྡུག་བསྔལ་བ་དང་། ​ཀུན་འབྱུང་བ་དང་། འགོག་པ་དང་ལམ་མ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། འདི་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཏེ། བདེན་པ་བཞི་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །བདེན་པ་ལ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་དང་། འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་བདེན་པའོ། །​དེ་ལ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བདེན་པ་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་ལ་ཀུན་འབྱུང་བ་དང་། རྒ་ཤིའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དུ་ཤེས་པའོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་། ཀུན་འབྱུང་དང་། འགོག་པ་དང་། ལམ་དུ་ཤེས་པའོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པ་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་ལ་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི། སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་བདེན་པ་ཤེས་པའོ། །​གང་གིས་སྲིད་པ་འཇོམས་པ་ནི་ཀུན་འབྱུང་གི་བདེན་པ་ཤེས་པའོ། །མ་རིག་པ་དང་། བག་ལ་ཉལ་བ་རྣམས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མེད་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འགོག་པའི་བདེན་པ་ཤེས་པའོ། །​ཆོས་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་དུ་རིང་བས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྒྲོ་མི་འདོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་ལམ་གྱི་བདེན་པ་ཤེས་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །​དེ་ལྟར་བདེན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་ན་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མེད་པས་ན་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
translation: Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ།
source: བདེན་པ་རྣམས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མེད་པར་ཅི་མངོན་ཞེ་ན།  འཕགས་པ་བློ་གྲོས་མི་ཟད་པའི་མདོ་ལས་བཤད་པ།  བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བདེན་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་གང་ཞེ་ན། ཕུང་པོ་འདི་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བ་སྟེ། གང་གིས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་མཚན་མ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་རྟོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །​གང་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་སྲེད་པའི་རྒྱུ་དང་ལྟ་བའི་རྒྱུ་ནི་ཀུན་འབྱུང་སྟེ། གང་གིས་སྲེད་པའི་རྒྱུ་དང་། ལྟ་བའི་རྒྱུ་དེ་དག་མི་ལེན་ཅིང་སྒྲོ་མི་འདོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་ཀུན་འབྱུང་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །​གང་ཕུང་པོ་སྔོན་གྱི་མཐའ་ཡང་མི་འབྱུང་། ཕྱི་མའི་མཐར་ཡང་མི་འཕོ། །​ད་ལྟར་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི་འགོག་པ་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །​གང་མི་གཉིས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་ནས་བདེན་པ་བཞི་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ནི། ལམ་འཕགས་པའི་བདེན་པ་ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །
translation: If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ།
translation: Regarding 'not pristine wisdom, not attainment, and also not non-attainment', concerning this, this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas. That pristine wisdom of abandoning the two, the afflictive obscuration and the cognitive obscuration, is called non-dual pristine wisdom; because ultimately it is not pristine wisdom, that pristine wisdom is said to be non-existent.

Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ།
translation: 'Attainment' means attaining from what was previously non-existent. Because if there is attainment, there is also emptiness, and if there is a result, it is subject to destruction, the intrinsic nature of a Buddha abides equally in all sentient beings; it is empty in the beginning and there is no attainment in the end. The mention of the sequence of the ten grounds is also merely the gradual purification of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness; once the latent tendencies of ignorance are purified, within the dharmadhātu, which is like the mirror of a Buddha's pristine wisdom, there is no imputing 'attainment' and 'non-attainment', and therefore attainment is also non-existent.

[1-43] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

[1-44] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།
translation: Non-attainment is also said to be non-existent. Therefore, it is also said in the Prajñāpāramitā in Seven Hundred Lines: 'Not engaging in any marks is engaging in prajñāpāramitā. Attaining nothing at all is attaining unsurpassable awakening.' These are the qualities of prajñāpāramitā. Although a yogi's unsurpassable awakening is the nature of emptiness, nevertheless, the result of the perfection is also not non-existent; the qualities are explained to generate enthusiasm, saying 'It exists'. Regarding 'Śāriputra, therefore, because bodhisattvas have no attainment, they abide in and rely on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Therefore' is as explained above. 'Because there is no attainment' is because there is no attaining the result of unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening.

Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

[1-45] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

[1-46] source:
​ཡེ་ཤེས་མ་ཡིན་ཐོབ་པ་མ་ཡིན། མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། དེ་ལ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། ​འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་ཞུགས་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ལོ། །དེ་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་དང་། ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་གཉིས་སྤང་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་གཉིས་སུ་མེད་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དོན་དམ་པར་ཡེ་ཤེས་མ་ཡིན་པས་ན་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །

That pristine wisdom of abandoning the two, the afflictive obscuration and the cognitive obscuration, is called non-dual pristine wisdom; because ultimately it is not pristine wisdom, that pristine wisdom is said to be non-existent.

ཐོབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྔོན་མེད་པ་ལས་ཐོབ་པའོ། །​ཐོབ་པ་ཡོད་ན་སྟོང་པ་ཡང་ཡོད་ལ། འབྲས་བུ་ཡོད་ན་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བས་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ནི། སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་ལ་མཉམ་པར་གནས་པ་དེ་ནི་ཐོག་མར་ཡང་སྟོང་། ཐ་མར་ཡང་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་དེ། ས་བཅུའི་རིམ་པ་སྨོས་པ་ཡང་ཀུན་གཞི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་རིམ་གྱིས་སྦྱང་བ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་དེ། ​མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་བྱང་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་མེ་ལོང་དང་འདྲ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ལ་ནི་ཐོབ་པ་དང་། མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཞེས་གདགས་སུ་མེད་པས་ན་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད།
[1-47] translation already produced for this document:
'Attainment' means attaining from what was previously non-existent. Because if there is attainment, there is also emptiness, and if there is a result, it is subject to destruction, the intrinsic nature of a Buddha abides equally in all sentient beings; it is empty in the beginning and there is no attainment in the end. The mention of the sequence of the ten grounds is also merely the gradual purification of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness; once the latent tendencies of ignorance are purified, within the dharmadhātu, which is like the mirror of a Buddha's pristine wisdom, there is no imputing 'attainment' and 'non-attainment', and therefore attainment is also non-existent.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།
translation: 'Having no obscuration of mind' is because the inner latent tendencies and all outer marks have been abandoned and are non-existent. Regarding 'having no fear', because there is thus no obscuration of mind, it is because there is no fear of being born in saṃsāra and the lower realms, and no fear regarding the meaning of profound phenomena having no birth and no cessation.

[1-43] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

[1-44] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. 'Attainment' means attaining from what was previously non-existent. Because if there is attainment, there is also emptiness, and if there is a result, it is subject to destruction, the intrinsic nature of a Buddha abides equally in all sentient beings; it is empty in the beginning and there is no attainment in the end. The mention of the sequence of the ten grounds is also merely the gradual purification of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness; once the latent tendencies of ignorance are purified, within the dharmadhātu, which is like the mirror of a Buddha's pristine wisdom, there is no imputing 'attainment' and 'non-attainment', and therefore attainment is also non-existent.

translation: Regarding 'completely passed beyond inverted views', viewing the non-existent outer objects of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness as various aspects is called 'inverted views'; by understanding the selflessness of persons and phenomena regarding this, and abandoning the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, one passes beyond inverted views.

Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

Because if there is attainment, there is also emptiness, and if there is a result, it is subject to destruction, the intrinsic nature of a Buddha abides equally in all sentient beings; it is empty in the beginning and there is no attainment in the end. heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན།
translation: Regarding 'attaining nirvāṇa', ignorance is the ground of all afflictions, and because it becomes the cause of saṃsāra even within the twelve links of dependent origination, it is said that 'finally an entire mass of suffering is assembled.' If one knows ignorance to be non-existent, suffering and all afflictions also become non-existent. Therefore, it is called 'attaining nirvāṇa'.

[1-43] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'not extinction of aging and death', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas. To state from ignorance up to aging and death is to speak in summary; from formations by the condition of ignorance, one should view up to consciousness, name and form, the six sense sources, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, existence, birth, and aging and death. 'Ignorance' means that karma arises through the view of self. Grasping at a self arises from non-entity; therefore, ignorance is also a non-entity. For example, if a house has remained in darkness for a long time, the appearance of a single lamp makes it instantly non-existent, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Similarly, the dense darkness of sentient beings' ignorance from beginningless time is made instantly non-existent when examined with the lamp of prajñā, and that non-existent entity is also not seen. Moreover, 'awareness' is merely imputed as the counterpart of ignorance; since ignorance is non-existent, the name of awareness is also not established, and therefore it is said 'not ignorance, not extinction of ignorance'. Because the entity of ignorance itself is non-existent, ignorance is non-existent. Because it does not appear like a non-existent entity, extinction is also said to be non-existent.

Regarding 'not suffering, origin, cessation, and path', this is what is said: This is the domain of practice of those who have entered the vehicle of the śrāvakas, which is called the four truths. Truths have three aspects: mundane, supramundane, and ultimate supramundane truths. Among these, mundane truth is knowing the five aggregates as the origin and as the suffering of aging and death. Supramundane truth is knowing suffering, origin, cessation, and path. Supramundane noble truth is knowing the five aggregates as having no birth, which is knowing the truth of suffering. Whatever conquers existence is knowing the truth of origin. Knowing ignorance and latent tendencies as non-existent by intrinsic nature is knowing the truth of cessation. By understanding phenomena as equality, not superimposing upon all things is called knowing the truth of the path. Thus, because the truths also ultimately do not exist by intrinsic nature, they are said to be 'not'.

If one asks, 'How is it evident that the truths are non-existent by intrinsic nature?', it is explained in the noble Akṣayamatinirdeśasūtra: 'What makes a bodhisattva skilled in the truths? These aggregates are suffering; whoever realizes the mark of suffering as emptiness just as it is, that is called the noble truth of suffering. The causes of craving and the causes of views concerning the five aggregates are the origin; whoever does not apprehend and does not superimpose those causes of craving and causes of views, that is called the noble truth of origin. Knowing that the aggregates do not arise in the past limit, do not transfer to the future limit, and do not remain in the present is called the noble truth of cessation. Whoever, resting evenly in non-dual pristine wisdom, knows the four truths as emptiness, that is explained as the noble truth of the path.'

མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་བདུན་བརྒྱ་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་།  མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་མི་སྤྱོད་པ་དེ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའོ། །​ཅི་ཡང་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །  འདི་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ནི་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཡིན་མོད་ཀྱི།  འོན་ཀྱང་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཡོད་དོ་ཞེས་སྤྲོ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡོན་ཏན་བཤད་དོ། །​  ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་གནས་ཤིང་བརྟེན་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་ནའོ། །​ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Attaining nothing at all is attaining unsurpassable awakening.' These are the qualities of prajñāpāramitā. Although a yogi's unsurpassable awakening is the nature of emptiness, nevertheless, the result of the perfection is also not non-existent; the qualities are explained to generate enthusiasm, saying 'It exists'. Regarding 'Śāriputra, therefore, because bodhisattvas have no attainment, they abide in and rely on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Therefore' is as explained above. 'Abiding in and relying on prajñāpāramitā' means not abiding in any marks.

[1-50] source:
སེམས་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ནང་གི་བག་ཆགས་དང་། ཕྱིའི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤངས་ཏེ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །​སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་མེད་པས་ན་འཁོར་བ་དང་ངན་སོང་དུ་སྐྱེ་བའི་འཇིགས་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་འགག་པ་མེད་པའི་དོན་ལ་འཇིགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[1-50] translation already produced for this document:
'Having no obscuration of mind' is because the inner latent tendencies and all outer marks have been abandoned and are non-existent. Regarding 'having no fear', because there is thus no obscuration of mind, it is because there is no fear of being born in saṃsāra and the lower realms, and no fear regarding the meaning of profound phenomena having no birth and no cessation.

[1-51] source:
ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལས་ཤིན་ཏུ་འདས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། ཀུན་གཞི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ཕྱི་རོལ་ཡུལ་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་ལྟ་བ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་ཆུད་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་། ​ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་སྤངས་ནས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལས་འདས་པའོ། །
[1-51] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'completely passed beyond inverted views', viewing the non-existent outer objects of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness as various aspects is called 'inverted views'; by understanding the selflessness of persons and phenomena regarding this, and abandoning the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, one passes beyond inverted views.

[1-52] source:
མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། མ་རིག་པ་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཀུན་གྱི་གཞི་སྟེ། རྟེན་འབྲེལ་ཡན་ལག་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ནང་ན་ཡང་འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱུར་འགྱུར་བས་ན་མཐའ་ནས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཀྱང་འདུས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །མ་རིག་པ་མེད་པར་ཤེས་ན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བ་དང་། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །​དེ་བས་ན་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
[1-52] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'attaining nirvāṇa', ignorance is the ground of all afflictions, and because it becomes the cause of saṃsāra even within the twelve links of dependent origination, it is said that 'finally an entire mass of suffering is assembled.' If one knows ignorance to be non-existent, suffering and all afflictions also become non-existent. Therefore, it is called 'attaining nirvāṇa'.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ།
source: དུས་གསུམ་དུ་རྣམ་པར་བཞུགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དུས་ནི་འདས་པ་དང་། མ་འོངས་པ་དང་། ད་ལྟར་གྱི་དུས་ཐ་དད་པ་རྣམས་སོ། །​བཞུགས་པ་ནི་དུས་གསུམ་དུ་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་སོ། །​སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་འཁོར་བའི་བསླད་པ་ལས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་མིག་ཐོབ་པས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དོན་དུ་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་གྱུར་ནས་ཤེས་རབ་དང་། ​ཡེ་ཤེས་དང་། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་དང་། མཚན་དང་། དཔེ་བྱད་དང་། མ་འདྲེས་པའི་ཆོས་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། ཡོན་ཏན་གྲངས་མེད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །​ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་པ་ལ་གནས་པས་སོ། །དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་མཚུངས་པར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་ན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཡུམ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
translation: Regarding 'all Buddhas who abide in the three times, having relied on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Times' refers to the distinct times of the past, future, and present. 'Abide' refers to those who have gone in the three times. 'Buddhas' are called 'buddhas' because they have attained the eye of prajñā out from the corruption of saṃsāra of the three realms; in reality, having become the dharmakāya, the perfection of innumerable qualities—such as prajñā, pristine wisdom, samādhi, the major marks, the minor signs, and the unshared qualities—is called a 'buddha'. 'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. Because all buddhas of the three times equally arise from prajñāpāramitā, this prajñāpāramitā is called the mother of all buddhas.

Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep mantra syllables and proper names in Sanskrit transliteration (Avalokiteśvara, Śāriputra, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.
context:
A canonical Tibetan Buddhist text, translated block by block from the critical edition in this vault. The blocks below are being translated in order.

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་སྙིང་པོའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (Praśāstrasena, Extensive Commentary on the Heart Sutra), author: སློབ་དཔོན་པྲ་ཤཱ་སྟྲ་སེ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[1-47] source:
ཐོབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྔོན་མེད་པ་ལས་ཐོབ་པའོ། །​ཐོབ་པ་ཡོད་ན་སྟོང་པ་ཡང་ཡོད་ལ། འབྲས་བུ་ཡོད་ན་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བས་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ནི། སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་ལ་མཉམ་པར་གནས་པ་དེ་ནི་ཐོག་མར་ཡང་སྟོང་། ཐ་མར་ཡང་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་དེ། ས་བཅུའི་རིམ་པ་སྨོས་པ་ཡང་ཀུན་གཞི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་རིམ་གྱིས་སྦྱང་བ་ཙམ་དུ་ཟད་དེ། ​མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་བྱང་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་མེ་ལོང་དང་འདྲ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ལ་ནི་ཐོབ་པ་དང་། མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཞེས་གདགས་སུ་མེད་པས་ན་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད།
[1-47] translation already produced for this document:
'Attainment' means attaining from what was previously non-existent. Because if there is attainment, there is also emptiness, and if there is a result, it is subject to destruction, the intrinsic nature of a Buddha abides equally in all sentient beings; it is empty in the beginning and there is no attainment in the end. The mention of the sequence of the ten grounds is also merely the gradual purification of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness; once the latent tendencies of ignorance are purified, within the dharmadhātu, which is like the mirror of a Buddha's pristine wisdom, there is no imputing 'attainment' and 'non-attainment', and therefore attainment is also non-existent.

[1-48] source:
མ་ཐོབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་བདུན་བརྒྱ་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་།  མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་མི་སྤྱོད་པ་དེ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའོ། །​ཅི་ཡང་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །  འདི་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ནི་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་ཡིན་མོད་ཀྱི།  འོན་ཀྱང་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཡོད་དོ་ཞེས་སྤྲོ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡོན་ཏན་བཤད་དོ། །​  ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་གནས་ཤིང་བརྟེན་ཏེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་གོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་ནའོ། །​ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[1-48] translation already produced for this document:
Non-attainment is also said to be non-existent. Therefore, it is also said in the Prajñāpāramitā in Seven Hundred Lines: 'Not engaging in any marks is engaging in prajñāpāramitā. Attaining nothing at all is attaining unsurpassable awakening.' These are the qualities of prajñāpāramitā. Although a yogi's unsurpassable awakening is the nature of emptiness, nevertheless, the result of the perfection is also not non-existent; the qualities are explained to generate enthusiasm, saying 'It exists'. Regarding 'Śāriputra, therefore, because bodhisattvas have no attainment, they abide in and rely on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Therefore' is as explained above. 'Because there is no attainment' is because there is no attaining the result of unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening.

[1-49] source:

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ།
translation: Regarding 'fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Unsurpassable' means having passed beyond the three realms. 'Perfectly complete' is the ultimate limit of phenomena, the unerring suchness. 'Awakening' is suchness, the dharmadhātu. 'Fully awaken' refers to having practiced prajñāpāramitā in a non-conceptual manner and having manifestly awakened, being no different from the buddhas of the past and being equal in qualities.

[1-47] translation already produced for this document:
'Attainment' means attaining from what was previously non-existent. Because if there is attainment, there is also emptiness, and if there is a result, it is subject to destruction, the intrinsic nature of a Buddha abides equally in all sentient beings; it is empty in the beginning and there is no attainment in the end. The mention of the sequence of the ten grounds is also merely the gradual purification of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness; once the latent tendencies of ignorance are purified, within the dharmadhātu, which is like the mirror of a Buddha's pristine wisdom, there is no imputing 'attainment' and 'non-attainment', and therefore attainment is also non-existent.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གཟུངས།
translation: This is the dhāraṇī of prajñā; it is stated in order not to fall. Therefore, regarding 'true and unerring', concerning this, this is what is said: Because there is no speaking with words, there is wishlessness; thus that is the truth of speech. Because there is no conduct of the body, there is signlessness; thus it is the truth of the body. Because there is no thinking of the mind, from emptiness it is the truth of the mind. Thus, it does not contradict the three gateways to noble liberation; and because prajñāpāramitā, having cleared away all marks of the mind, accords with the meaning of non-conceptuality, the gateway of simultaneous entry into the ultimate, it is true and unerring. Because it clears away all inner latent tendencies of consciousness, it is the mantra of prajñāpāramitā.

'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. [1-54] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'all Buddhas who abide in the three times, having relied on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Times' refers to the distinct times of the past, future, and present. 'Abide' refers to those who have gone in the three times. 'Buddhas' are called 'buddhas' because they have attained the eye of prajñā out from the corruption of saṃsāra of the three realms; in reality, having become the dharmakāya, the perfection of innumerable qualities—such as prajñā, pristine wisdom, samādhi, the major marks, the minor signs, and the unshared qualities—is called a 'buddha'. 'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. Because all buddhas of the three times equally arise from prajñāpāramitā, this prajñāpāramitā is called the mother of all buddhas.

Regarding 'fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Unsurpassable' means having passed beyond the three realms. 'Perfectly complete' is the ultimate limit of phenomena, the unerring suchness. 'Awakening' is suchness, the dharmadhātu. 'Fully awaken' refers to having practiced prajñāpāramitā in a non-conceptual manner and having manifestly awakened, being no different from the buddhas of the past and being equal in qualities.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གཟུངས།
translation: Because it clears away all marks of both outer and inner, it is the unsurpassable mantra.

Regarding 'all Buddhas who abide in the three times, having relied on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Times' refers to the distinct times of the past, future, and present. 'Abide' refers to those who have gone in the three times. 'Buddhas' are called 'buddhas' because they have attained the eye of prajñā out from the corruption of saṃsāra of the three realms; in reality, having become the dharmakāya, the perfection of innumerable qualities—such as prajñā, pristine wisdom, samādhi, the major marks, the minor signs, and the unshared qualities—is called a 'buddha'. 'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. Because all buddhas of the three times equally arise from prajñāpāramitā, this prajñāpāramitā is called the mother of all buddhas.

Regarding 'fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Unsurpassable' means having passed beyond the three realms. 'Perfectly complete' is the ultimate limit of phenomena, the unerring suchness. 'Awakening' is suchness, the dharmadhātu. 'Fully awaken' refers to having practiced prajñāpāramitā in a non-conceptual manner and having manifestly awakened, being no different from the buddhas of the past and being equal in qualities.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གཟུངས།
translation: Because it abandons all lower realms and accomplishes the benefit of sentient beings, it is the mantra that completely pacifies all suffering.

'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. [1-52] source:

Work: འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་སྙིང་པོའི་རྒྱ་ཆེར་འགྲེལ་པ། (Praśāstrasena, Extensive Commentary on the Heart Sutra), author: སློབ་དཔོན་པྲ་ཤཱ་སྟྲ་སེ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[1-50] source:
སེམས་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ནང་གི་བག་ཆགས་དང་། ཕྱིའི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤངས་ཏེ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །​སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྒྲིབ་པ་མེད་པས་ན་འཁོར་བ་དང་ངན་སོང་དུ་སྐྱེ་བའི་འཇིགས་པ་དང་། ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་སྐྱེ་བ་དང་འགག་པ་མེད་པའི་དོན་ལ་འཇིགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[1-50] translation already produced for this document:
'Having no obscuration of mind' is because the inner latent tendencies and all outer marks have been abandoned and are non-existent. Regarding 'having no fear', because there is thus no obscuration of mind, it is because there is no fear of being born in saṃsāra and the lower realms, and no fear regarding the meaning of profound phenomena having no birth and no cessation.

[1-51] source:
ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལས་ཤིན་ཏུ་འདས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། ཀུན་གཞི་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ཕྱི་རོལ་ཡུལ་དངོས་པོ་མེད་པ་ལ་རྣམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་སུ་ལྟ་བ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ལ་བདག་མེད་པར་ཆུད་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་། ​ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་སྤངས་ནས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ལས་འདས་པའོ། །
[1-51] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'completely passed beyond inverted views', viewing the non-existent outer objects of the latent tendencies of ignorance in the all-ground consciousness as various aspects is called 'inverted views'; by understanding the selflessness of persons and phenomena regarding this, and abandoning the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, one passes beyond inverted views.

[1-52] source:
མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། མ་རིག་པ་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཀུན་གྱི་གཞི་སྟེ། རྟེན་འབྲེལ་ཡན་ལག་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ནང་ན་ཡང་འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱུར་འགྱུར་བས་ན་མཐའ་ནས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཀྱང་འདུས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །མ་རིག་པ་མེད་པར་ཤེས་ན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བ་དང་། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །​དེ་བས་ན་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
[1-52] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'attaining nirvāṇa', ignorance is the ground of all afflictions, and because it becomes the cause of saṃsāra even within the twelve links of dependent origination, it is said that 'finally an entire mass of suffering is assembled.' If one knows ignorance to be non-existent, suffering and all afflictions also become non-existent. Therefore, it is called 'attaining nirvāṇa'.

[1-53] source:
འདི་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་སྟེ། ​འབྲས་བུ་མེད་ན་སྤྱད་པ་ཡང་དོན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྲས་བུ་བཤད་དོ། །​
[1-53] translation already produced for this document:
This is the result of prajñāpāramitā; because if there were no result, the practice would also be meaningless, the result is explained.

[1-54] source:
དུས་གསུམ་དུ་རྣམ་པར་བཞུགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ། འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དུས་ནི་འདས་པ་དང་། མ་འོངས་པ་དང་། ད་ལྟར་གྱི་དུས་ཐ་དད་པ་རྣམས་སོ། །​བཞུགས་པ་ནི་དུས་གསུམ་དུ་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་སོ། །​སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་འཁོར་བའི་བསླད་པ་ལས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་མིག་ཐོབ་པས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱ་སྟེ། དོན་དུ་ན་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་གྱུར་ནས་ཤེས་རབ་དང་། ​ཡེ་ཤེས་དང་། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་དང་། མཚན་དང་། དཔེ་བྱད་དང་། མ་འདྲེས་པའི་ཆོས་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྟེ། ཡོན་ཏན་གྲངས་མེད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །​ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ཐམས་ཅད་མེད་པ་ལ་གནས་པས་སོ། །དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་མཚུངས་པར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་ན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཡུམ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
[1-54] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'all Buddhas who abide in the three times, having relied on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Times' refers to the distinct times of the past, future, and present. 'Abide' refers to those who have gone in the three times. 'Buddhas' are called 'buddhas' because they have attained the eye of prajñā out from the corruption of saṃsāra of the three realms; in reality, having become the dharmakāya, the perfection of innumerable qualities—such as prajñā, pristine wisdom, samādhi, the major marks, the minor signs, and the unshared qualities—is called a 'buddha'. 'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. Because all buddhas of the three times equally arise from prajñāpāramitā, this prajñāpāramitā is called the mother of all buddhas.

[1-55] source:
​བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སངས་རྒྱས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བྱ་སྟེ། བླ་ན་མེད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཁམས་གསུམ་ལས་འདས་པའོ། །​ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། ​དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མ་ནོར་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་མཐར་ཐུག་པའོ། །​བྱང་ཆུབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་སོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་སོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་སྤྱད་ནས་མངོན་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཏེ་འདས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་དང་ཡང་མི་འདྲ་བ་མེད་པ་དང་། ཡོན་ཏན་མཚུངས་པ་ལ་བྱའོ། །
[1-55] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding 'fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Unsurpassable' means having passed beyond the three realms. 'Perfectly complete' is the ultimate limit of phenomena, the unerring suchness. 'Awakening' is suchness, the dharmadhātu. 'Fully awaken' refers to having practiced prajñāpāramitā in a non-conceptual manner and having manifestly awakened, being no different from the buddhas of the past and being equal in qualities.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གཟུངས།
translation: Tadyathā: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Heart Sūtra (Prajñāpāramitā Hṛdaya) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep mantra syllables and proper names in Sanskrit transliteration (Avalokiteśvara, Śāriputra, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own.

[1-52] source:

འདི་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་སྟེ། ​འབྲས་བུ་མེད་ན་སྤྱད་པ་ཡང་དོན་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་འབྲས་བུ་བཤད་དོ། །​

Regarding 'all Buddhas who abide in the three times, having relied on prajñāpāramitā', concerning this, this is what is said: 'Times' refers to the distinct times of the past, future, and present. 'Abide' refers to those who have gone in the three times. 'Buddhas' are called 'buddhas' because they have attained the eye of prajñā out from the corruption of saṃsāra of the three realms; in reality, having become the dharmakāya, the perfection of innumerable qualities—such as prajñā, pristine wisdom, samādhi, the major marks, the minor signs, and the unshared qualities—is called a 'buddha'. 'Relying on prajñāpāramitā' is because of abiding in the absence of all marks. Because all buddhas of the three times equally arise from prajñāpāramitā, this prajñāpāramitā is called the mother of all buddhas.

'Fully awaken' refers to having practiced prajñāpāramitā in a non-conceptual manner and having manifestly awakened, being no different from the buddhas of the past and being equal in qualities.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གཟུངས།
translation: This mantra of prajñāpāramitā becomes the cause of mundane and supramundane merit. Mundane merit means that one is unharmed by afflictions, māras, and obstructors, and is able to be protected. Supramundane merit is that, by relying on this dhāraṇī, it becomes the cause of prajñā and jñāna.

heading: ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གཟུངས།
translation: Regarding 'Then the Bhagavan also arose from that samādhi', concerning this, this is what is said: Except for the Tathāgata alone, others are not able to explain and listen to the meaning of prajñāpāramitā; therefore, noble Avalokiteśvara explaining and Śāriputra listening were also the blessing of that samādhi. Since the actions of explaining and listening had been done, he arose from that samādhi.
